title: Seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–35)
hookLine: the same apology, on repeat. Peter wants a number
tomorrow: why would Jesus' own friends shoo the children away?

cards: Some hurts come back on repeat: the same late text, the same forgotten promise, the same eye-roll. Peter wants to know how long he has to keep forgiving.
So he asks for a number, and offers a generous one: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
Jesus answers: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Then he tells a story about why the counting won't work.

teach.b: A king settles accounts. One servant owes ten thousand talents, a debt no one could ever pay. He falls down and begs: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all."
And the king does more than wait. He "was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt." All of it.
That same servant walks out, finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred pence, and grabs him by the throat: "Pay me that thou owest."
The man begs him in almost the same words: have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. He won't hear it, and throws him in prison.
The king calls him back: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" Here's what this week might need from it.

The servant had been forgiven everything and still couldn't forgive a little, because he never let the first mercy change him. And notice what Jesus does not say. The same chapter began with naming the fault out loud.
Forgiving again isn't pretending it never happened.
Seventy times seven isn't a bigger number to track. It's the end of tracking.

how: Christians pray 'forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors' in the Lord's Prayer, and some churches read this parable when they teach about forgiveness.

o: a fixed limit on how often to forgive
a prophecy counting years until the end

games.q: the unforgiving servant — tap the pairs.
p: the debt the servant wouldn't forgive

s: seventy times seven means you can stop forgiving after 490
the story that follows is about ending the count, not reaching it.
the fellow servant begged in almost the same words the first servant used
have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.

games.q: a coworker covered for you on a huge mistake last month. today a new hire gets your order wrong, and you're about to snap. what would the parable ask first?
o: remember what was forgiven you, and let it change how you answer.
point out the mistake firmly, so it doesn't happen again.
say nothing now, and keep a note in case it happens twice.
games.why: the servant forgiven ten thousand talents wouldn't forgive a hundred pence. the king's question: shouldest not thou also have had compassion?

practice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper. Write the initial of someone you've had to forgive for the same thing more than once, and under it, two words: and again.
Fold it and hold it in your hand for the sit; it's not a promise to feel anything yet, just the start of not counting.

wordCard.voice: Seventy times seven. Jesus' answer to Peter's count: not a bigger number, the end of the ledger.

orig.note: Greek: to forgive, to let go; the verb in Peter's question in Matthew 18:21.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: and again, because the king forgave the whole debt first. That’s today.
